clue.text: (& 15ac.) Exotic fan dance in decline – pine for an alternative to living off the British taxpayer?

definitions.text: an alternative to living off the British taxpayer?

indicators.note: something exotic is strange and unfamiliar, so the letters come out in an unfamiliar order

blocks.note: taken as written, letters for mixing
taken as written, letters for mixing

explanation.surface: A tired striptease act is on the way out, and the performer longs for a way to stop being kept by the public purse.
explanation.walkthrough: All twenty-one letters of 'fan dance in decline' and 'pine' are rearranged. The surface glances at royals (Harry and Meghan in 2020) who said they wanted to stop being funded by the Sovereign Grant.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying your own way, rather than relying on public money, is exactly what having enough money of your own provides.

clue.text: No-fly cruises centre bust? I wish!

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its single middle letter, which is all that is kept
something bust is broken, so the letters are broken up and put back together differently

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the hyphen
the fourth of seven letters sits in the middle

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker who refuses to fly dreams of a cruise that is a flop, or perhaps of a bust at the centre of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cruises centre' looks like a phrase about holidays, but it simply supplies the middle letter of cruises.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions voice a longing for something that is not the case; one is a common replacement for the other in speech.

clue.text: see 6dn.
Bed with minimum of bed linen, a help to a cheat?

blocks.note: a crib is a baby's bed
the least bed linen you could have is a single one of these

explanation.surface: A sparsely made bed, barely any linen on it, somehow helping someone to cheat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minimum of' looks like it wants a first letter, but here it means the smallest possible amount of bed linen: one piece of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A student hides a page of crammed notes in an exam to copy answers from, which aids dishonest test-taking.

clue.text: Royal sprog all over Victor's record collection

indicators.note: to be all over something is to cover it completely, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: Archie is the son of Prince Harry and Meghan; a sprog is British slang for a baby
V is Victor in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A royal toddler has got all over Victor's precious vinyl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record collection' suggests vinyl but means stored documents. The 's of Victor's is just the possessive of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A set of historical documents and records kept together is the sense here, so a store of records fits.

clue.text: (& 3dn./22dn.)Arguments on both sides for Boris's ultimate 'plus' with party members

indicators.note: ultimate means final, so only the last letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: pro is Latin for 'for', as in pro-choice
the final letter of the name
plus and and both mean in addition
Cons is short for Conservatives, Boris Johnson's party

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson's last push with his Tory colleagues, framed as balanced debate.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spreads across three lights (6ac, 3dn, 22dn).
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the standard idiom for the points in favour of and against a proposal.

clue.text: Like a corner of true England pointlessly ballsed up

indicators.note: a point here is a compass point, so being without one means a letter like N, S, E or W is removed
something ballsed up is made a mess of, so its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: true and right both mean correct
taken as written; one N, a compass point, is then dropped

explanation.surface: A gripe that some corner of true-blue England has been pointlessly mucked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointlessly' looks like an adverb about futility; it removes the N (north) from ENGLAND, and the remaining EGLAND is mixed to ANGLED.
explanation.definitionFit: A typical corner meets at ninety degrees, so describing it with this adjective is a natural description of its shape.

clue.text: Piss taken in hospital?

blocks.note: surface reading: taking the piss, British slang for mocking someone
setter's reading: urine literally collected from a patient for testing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking the piss' is British slang for mockery, so the clue seems to be about teasing on a ward; read literally it is a urine sample.
explanation.definitionFit: A sample of urine handed over for laboratory analysis is the standard medical term for such material.

clue.text: see 25ac.
Record success in faking old discovery

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words, spanning their letters

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of faking through old into the start of discovery

explanation.surface: A celebrated old find turns out to have been forged — a record-breaking fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record success' reads like a record-breaking achievement but means a hit music record.
explanation.definitionFit: Artists receive this award when an album or single sells a set number of copies, marking a hit record.

clue.text: A potential hooker's view, right?

blocks.note: an angle is a point of view
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Asking for a prostitute's perspective, with a tag question on the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooker' suggests a prostitute but means someone who hooks a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fishing with rod and line hopes to catch fish on a hook, so they are a would-be hooker.

clue.text: Casual wear left in beds

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: the sack is slang for bed, as in hit the sack
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Leisure clothes abandoned on the beds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb (left behind) but is just L.
explanation.definitionFit: These are loose informal trousers, a classic item of leisure clothing.

clue.text: A European as opposed to a Brit?

definitions.text: A European as opposed to a Brit?

blocks.note: surface reading: Britons are Europeans too, so the contrast looks odd, a dig at Brexit
setter's reading: the British word for someone from mainland Europe rather than the islands

explanation.walkthrough: Britons habitually speak of 'the Continent' meaning mainland Europe, as though Britain were not part of Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: British speakers use this noun for a person from mainland Europe, distinct from those living on the British Isles.

clue.text: Spot topless rose satin shifts

indicators.note: without a top, so the first letter of the word is removed
the letters shift position into a new order

blocks.note: rose is a shade of pink; its first letter is then dropped
taken as written, letters for mixing

explanation.surface: Spotting a topless woman in rose-coloured satin slips — Private Eye's brand of smut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shifts' reads as a noun (slips of satin) but is the verb that rearranges SATIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A blot or mark left on paper or cloth by spilt writing fluid is a kind of spot.

clue.text: see 1ac.
Depression surrounding Spielberg's film blunder is an obstacle

indicators.note: to surround something is to enclose it on all sides, so one piece goes around others

blocks.note: a dent is a small hollow or depression
E.T. is Steven Spielberg's 1982 film
to err is to make a mistake

explanation.surface: Gloom over a Spielberg movie flop proves a hurdle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' suggests low mood, but here it is a physical hollow, like one knocked into a car door.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that discourages or prevents action stands in the way, making it a kind of barrier or hindrance.

clue.text: Go in pants to rave, not having a clue

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are made a mess of

blocks.note: taken as written, letters for mixing
to rave is to rant wildly

explanation.surface: Turning up to a rave in just your underwear, clueless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like underwear (British for underpants) but is slang for rubbish, signalling a jumble of GO IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking knowledge or awareness is what it means to be without any idea, the idiom of not having a clue.

clue.text: Enter a Southern English town and start scrapping

blocks.note: to enter is to go into
Battle is a town in East Sussex, near the site of the 1066 battle of Hastings

explanation.surface: Arriving in a south-coast town and immediately picking a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The town really is called Battle, named after the Battle of Hastings fought there.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrapping is informal for fighting, so beginning to scrap is to commence combat.

clue.text: Interferes when arses get elected

blocks.note: butts is slang for backsides
a party that is elected is in

explanation.surface: A cynical political jibe: idiots win office and start meddling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arses' in British slang also means idiots, which drives the political surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To intrude uninvited into others' business is to meddle, which is what interfering means.

clue.text: Balls take a bashing in this perverted vice trap

definitions.text: Balls take a bashing in this

indicators.note: to pervert is literally to turn the wrong way, so the letters are turned back to front

blocks.note: a vice is a sin
a net is a trap

explanation.surface: A lurid tabloid line about a sex den where balls get a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a kinky scandal; the definition is innocent once balls are sporting ones.
explanation.definitionFit: In this racket sport players strike balls hard over a net, so the balls are repeatedly hit.

clue.text: Crew up to mischief, which is disruptive, currently

indicators.note: being up to mischief means causing havoc, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, letters for mixing

explanation.surface: A gang of troublemakers causing a nuisance at the moment.

tit as a teat; an udder is the milk gland bearing teats

clue.text: Funny thing, abandoning 'love' box

clue.text: (& 9dn.) Action of pissed off royals? A way to get Essex town "tail"

Epping is a town in Essex, England, near Epping Forest

clue.text: (& 27ac.) Exercise and start to produce gas – it's supposed to be arousing

the opening letter

clue.text: see 26dn.
At evening's end, Stan sips sloppy, crap booze

blocks.note: the closing letter
taken as written, letters for mixing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnat's piss' is British slang for a weak, tasteless drink, usually beer.
